title.rendered: A Member Portal That Doesn’t Bill Per Member

excerpt.rendered: What a flat-fee member portal actually includes — dues, renewals, events, and directory access — built to sync with your existing AMS.

content.rendered:
Most association management systems (AMS) sell member-facing portal access as an add-on priced by active member count, by portal login, or by a tier tied to total membership size. That’s the opposite of what an association wants: portal adoption going up is the goal, and a pricing model that charges more for higher adoption fights against it. Here’s what a purpose-built, flat-fee member portal actually contains and how it’s built.

What goes in the portal

  • Dues and renewal status — members see what’s owed and pay online, synced back to the AMS as the record of truth.
  • Event registration — chapter and national event sign-up without a separate ticketing tool’s per-registration fee.
  • Member directory — searchable, with privacy controls members manage themselves.
  • Digital membership card / ID — for chapters and associations that use member ID for benefits or event check-in.
  • Document library — bylaws, certificates, CE credit records, whatever the association’s members repeatedly request from staff.

How it connects to your AMS

The portal is a client-facing front end synced live to your existing AMS through its API — the AMS stays the system of record for membership data, dues, and history. Staff keep working in the AMS exactly as before; the portal changes what members see, not what your team runs on.

AMS-native member portal add-on Third-party portal tool Custom-built portal
Pricing Often per active member or tiered by total membership Separate subscription, its own tier ceiling One flat monthly fee
Cost as membership grows Rises Rises Unchanged
Feature fit Vendor-defined, generic across associations Vendor-defined Built to your specific chapter/dues structure
Build timeline N/A — already exists N/A — already exists Weeks, not months, for an ARDN build

Why this differs from an internal AMS seat problem

This is the member-facing side of the equation, distinct from staff seat costs inside the AMS itself. If your association is also paying per-seat for internal staff users, that’s a separate lever — see cutting AMS per-seat costs for the internal-side fix. Chapters billing dues per member at the chapter level are a related but distinct problem covered in chapter management and per-member fees.

Rollout: what a build actually looks like

A member portal build starts with mapping which AMS fields and workflows the portal needs (dues status, event catalog, directory fields, document types), then building against the AMS’s API in parallel with staff continuing to use the AMS unchanged. Cutover for members happens once the portal is validated against real account data — not a hard switch that risks member-facing downtime.

See what ARDN builds specifically for membership organizations at membership management, scope a custom portal for your association, or model the numbers with the savings calculator.

Frequently asked questions

Does a flat-fee portal mean unlimited members?

Yes — that’s the structural difference from per-seat or per-active-member pricing. The fee is set for the build and its ongoing operation, not for a headcount that has to be tracked and re-billed as membership changes.

Can it handle multiple chapters or membership tiers?

Yes, when it’s built to your structure from the start — chapter-specific views, tiered benefit visibility, and role-based directory access are scoping decisions made up front, not limitations of the flat-fee model.

What happens to our AMS if we add a custom portal?

Nothing changes about it. The AMS keeps running as your system of record; the portal reads and writes to it through the API. Staff workflows inside the AMS are unaffected.

title.rendered: An IT Director’s Guide to Consolidating Shadow SaaS

excerpt.rendered: A step-by-step playbook for IT directors to find, classify, and consolidate shadow SaaS tools before the next renewal cycle.

content.rendered:
Knowing shadow IT exists is not the same as having a plan to deal with it. This is the operational playbook for an IT director running that project end to end: discovery, classification, the consolidation decision, and rollout — the part that actually gets tool count and per-seat spend down instead of just documenting it.

Step 1: Run discovery across three sources at once

Source What it catches
SSO / identity provider connected-app report Anything employees signed into with company credentials
Expensed card and AP statements Anything paid for directly, bypassing SSO entirely
Network/CASB traffic logs (if available) Tools used without any company login at all

Run all three in parallel rather than sequentially — the point is to cross-reference them, since a tool that appears on the card statement but not the SSO list is a different kind of risk than one that appears on both.

Step 2: Classify, don’t just list

  • Sanctioned-worthy — solves a real problem well, low risk, formalize it with a proper contract and admin ownership.
  • Overlapping — duplicates a capability already covered by an approved system; a consolidation candidate.
  • High-risk, low-value — handles sensitive data with no security review and marginal actual use; retire first.
  • Dormant — still billing, barely used; cancel immediately, no consolidation project needed.

Step 3: Build the consolidation business case per cluster

Group overlapping tools by the workflow they serve (client status views, internal dashboards, intake forms) rather than by department. A cluster of three $15-30/seat tools doing variations of the same job is usually a stronger case for a single custom-built replacement than any one of them is for a point-solution swap, because the flat monthly fee replaces the combined per-seat bill of all three at once.

Step 4: Sequence the rollout to minimize disruption

Start with the cluster where the case is strongest and the user group is smallest — proving the model on a contained group before asking a bigger team to change habits. Migrate data and workflows in parallel with the old tools still live, then cut over once the replacement is validated, rather than a hard-cutover on a single date.

Step 5: Close the loop so shadow SaaS doesn’t come back

Discovery without an ongoing process just resets to zero at the next renewal cycle. Put a recurring quarterly pull of the same three sources on the calendar, and route new tool requests through a lightweight approval step instead of a full procurement gate that pushes people back to buying quietly.

For the cost mechanics behind why this matters, see shadow IT: the per-seat cost you’re not tracking. To put a number on a specific consolidation, use the savings calculator, or see how continuous license monitoring works with License Guard.

Frequently asked questions

Should IT lead this alone, or bring in finance?

Bring finance in at Step 3 — they usually hold the AP data IT needs for discovery, and having them validate the business case up front makes the consolidation approval faster later.

What if a team resists giving up their shadow tool?

Ask what specific feature they’d lose in a consolidation, not whether they like the current tool. Most resistance is habit, not a genuine feature gap, and naming the gap explicitly either surfaces a real requirement to build for or resolves the objection.

How long does a full consolidation project typically take?

It depends on the number of clusters and how entrenched each tool is, but sequencing by smallest-user-group-first (Step 4) means the first win is usually visible in weeks, not months, even while later clusters are still in progress.

title.rendered: Shadow IT: The Per-Seat Cost You’re Not Tracking

excerpt.rendered: Shadow IT tools bought outside procurement quietly rack up per-seat fees mid-market companies never see coming until the audit.

content.rendered:
Shadow IT is any software a team pays for without IT or procurement signing off on it — a marketing team’s reporting tool, a sales rep’s prospecting add-on, an ops team’s project tracker. None of it shows up in a single line item, which is exactly why it’s expensive: every one of those tools bills per seat, and per-seat costs on tools nobody is tracking grow without anyone noticing.

Why mid-market companies are the most exposed

Companies in the 200-2,000 employee range sit in the worst spot for this. They’re big enough that individual managers have a card and the authority to buy a $15/seat tool without a procurement review, but not big enough to have a dedicated SaaS-management function watching for it. Enterprises have procurement gates; small companies have few enough tools that someone just knows what’s running. Mid-market is where visibility gaps are widest.

How the cost compounds silently

  • Team growth multiplies it automatically. A shadow tool at $20/seat for 8 people becomes $20/seat for 25 people as the team hires, with no one re-evaluating the tool or the price along the way.
  • Duplicate tools stack. Two teams often adopt overlapping tools independently because neither knew the other had already solved the same problem.
  • Renewals auto-escalate. Shadow subscriptions renew on a manager’s card with no one reviewing the new-year price increase against actual usage.

Where shadow IT actually hides

Source Why it’s invisible
Expensed company cards Shows up as a line item, not a licensing category, in expense reports
Free-tier-to-paid upgrades Started as a free trial a manager approved informally, then auto-upgraded
SSO-connected apps Employees connect apps via “Sign in with Google/Microsoft” without a purchase order
Per-team departmental budgets Approved locally, never rolled up into a company-wide software register

Finding it before it finds you at renewal

Your SSO or identity provider’s connected-app list is usually the single best source, since most shadow tools get connected through it even when they were never formally procured. Pair that with a pass through expensed card statements for recurring software charges. For the full step-by-step process, see how to run a SaaS spend audit.

The structural fix, not just visibility

Finding shadow IT is step one; the recurring problem is that most of what teams reach for shadow tools to do — a lightweight dashboard, a client-facing status view, a simple intake form — is exactly the kind of narrow, repetitive workflow a custom-built tool handles on one flat monthly fee instead of a per-seat subscription that grows with headcount. Consolidating three or four shadow tools into one purpose-built system, run for a flat fee, often costs less than what any single one of them was already billing.

Model what consolidating a specific shadow tool would save with the savings calculator.

Frequently asked questions

Is shadow IT always a security risk?

Not automatically, but it’s always a visibility risk — data living in a tool IT doesn’t know about can’t be secured, backed up, or governed to the same standard as sanctioned systems. The cost problem and the risk problem usually get fixed in the same pass.

How much shadow IT does a typical mid-market company have?

It varies too much by company to cite a universal figure honestly — what’s consistent is that the first formal audit almost always turns up more tools than IT expected. Run your own audit rather than benchmarking against a number that may not reflect your org.

Should every shadow tool just be shut down?

No — some solve a real problem well and are worth formally adopting. The goal is visibility and a deliberate decision per tool: keep it sanctioned, consolidate it into something else, or retire it — not a blanket ban that pushes teams back into buying things quietly.

Policyholders increasingly expect self-service: pulling a certificate of insurance, checking a claim status, downloading a policy document, without calling or emailing the agency. Building that experience through most agency management systems (AMS) means either a client-facing module priced per active user, or a bolt-on tool with its own subscription — both of which reintroduce per-seat economics on the exact group (clients) whose count you don’t control and don’t want to cap.

Why client counts make per-seat pricing the wrong fit here

Client-facing access is different from internal seat licensing in one important way: you want more clients using self-service, not fewer. Every other lever in this space (reclaiming dormant internal seats, right-sizing tiers) assumes you’re trying to shrink or control a count. Client self-service adoption is a number you’re actively trying to grow — which makes a per-user license fee for it directly counterproductive.

What a flat-fee client portal covers

  • Policy documents and ID cards — self-service download instead of an email request to a CSR.
  • Certificate of insurance requests — a common, repetitive request that ties up staff time when it comes in by phone or email.
  • Claim status visibility — read access to where a claim stands, synced from the AMS.
  • Payment and renewal status — visibility without requiring a call to the agency.

A custom client portal synced live to your AMS delivers this on one flat monthly fee — whether a hundred clients use it or ten thousand.

AMS-native client module Third-party client portal add-on Custom portal
Pricing Often per active client user Separate subscription, often tiered Flat monthly fee

The staff-time case, not just the license case

Beyond licensing, self-service shifts certificate and status requests off CSR phone and email queues entirely, freeing that time for actual servicing and sales work. That operational case often matters as much as the licensing math, especially for agencies where CSR time is the real constraint on growth.

Yes, a custom build is scoped to your specific carriers and document types rather than a generic template, which is often where off-the-shelf client portals fall short.

What about security for sensitive policy and claims data?

Access controls and data handling are built to the same standards your agency already applies to client data — self-service doesn’t mean loosening who can see what.

title.rendered: How to Run a SaaS Spend Audit

excerpt.rendered: A practical, step-by-step process for auditing SaaS spend across your company — before deciding what to cut, downgrade, or restructure.

content.rendered:
Most mid-market companies don’t have a single, accurate list of what they’re paying for software and who’s actually using it — spend is spread across procurement records, expensed cards, and whatever IT remembers approving. A proper audit fixes that visibility gap before any cost decision gets made, and it’s a more mechanical process than it sounds.

Step 1: Build the inventory

Pull every recurring software charge from finance/AP records, expensed card statements, and your SSO/identity provider’s connected-app list — the SSO list often catches shadow-IT tools nobody formally procured. Cross-reference the three sources; the gaps between them are informative on their own.

Step 2: Get license and seat counts per tool

For each tool above a meaningful spend threshold, pull the current licensed seat count and the license tier each user is on. This is usually available in the vendor’s own admin console (Salesforce Setup, HubSpot settings, etc.).

Step 3: Pull usage data, not assumptions

Seat count tells you what you’re paying for; login and feature-usage data tells you what you’re actually using. Export last-login dates and, where available, feature-level usage per seat. This step is what turns “we have 400 licenses” into “120 of those haven’t logged in this quarter.”

Step 4: Classify every seat

Classification Signal Action
Dormant No login in 60-90+ days Freeze, then reclaim
Over-licensed Active, but only using basic features Downgrade tier
Light/narrow user Active, but touches one narrow workflow repeatedly Candidate for flat-fee portal
Core user Active, using full feature set daily Keep full seat

Step 5: Quantify and prioritize

Multiply seat count by per-seat cost for each category to see where the real money sits. Dormant and over-licensed seats are usually the fastest win; light/narrow users are where the bigger structural savings live, because that group’s cost keeps growing with headcount indefinitely unless the model changes.

Step 6: Act on the biggest lever first

Reclaim dormant seats and downgrade over-licensed ones immediately — low risk, fast payoff. For light/narrow users, evaluate moving them to a custom flat-fee portal synced to your core system, which is the move that stops the bill from scaling with headcount rather than just trimming today’s number. See reducing CRM licensing costs for the CRM-specific version of this same audit, and a CFO’s guide to cutting software costs for how this fits a broader cost strategy.

Frequently asked questions

How often should a SaaS spend audit be repeated?

Quarterly is a reasonable cadence for manual audits; some tools (like License Guard for Salesforce) automate the dormant/duplicate detection continuously so the audit doesn’t fully reset to zero each quarter.

What’s the biggest blind spot in most audits?

Shadow IT — tools expensed on individual cards or approved informally that never entered a central procurement record. The SSO connected-app list is usually the best single source for catching these.

Do we need special software to run this audit?

No — a spreadsheet and access to each vendor’s admin console and your identity provider is enough for a first pass. Dedicated SaaS-management tools can automate parts of this at scale, but they’re not required to get started.

title.rendered: The Real Cost of Salesforce Partner Communities

excerpt.rendered: Experience Cloud partner licenses bill per external login. Here’s what that actually costs as your partner network grows, and the flat-fee alternative.

content.rendered:
A Salesforce partner community (built on Experience Cloud) is a common way to give resellers, brokers, dealers, or franchisees access to deal registration, inventory, or account data without handing them a full internal seat. It’s the right instinct — external users shouldn’t get internal licenses — but the license model underneath still bills per login, and partner networks have a habit of growing faster than anyone budgeted for.

How partner community licensing actually works

Experience Cloud partner licenses are sold in login-based or member-based models, priced well below an internal Sales/Service Cloud seat but still per-user. The math that catches teams off guard: a partner network isn’t static headcount like an internal team. Add ten new dealers or brokers this quarter and the license bill moves immediately, with no equivalent revenue-per-partner assumption built into the budget.

Where the cost creeps in

  • Partner turnover. Reseller and broker relationships churn — new partners onboard, old ones go dormant, and licenses often don’t get cleaned up in between.
  • Seasonal or low-activity partners. A dealer who logs in twice a quarter to check an order status is billed the same as one who lives in the portal daily.
  • Growth by design. If partner growth is the actual growth strategy — more resellers, more franchisees — the per-seat model taxes your own success.

The structural alternative: a portal, not a community license

What most partners actually need is narrow: check deal status, register a lead, pull inventory, download a spec sheet. That’s a smaller surface area than the full Experience Cloud community license assumes. A custom partner portal built to that exact scope, synced live to Salesforce as the system of record, replaces the per-login fee with one flat monthly fee — whether you have 20 partners or 200.

Experience Cloud partner community Custom partner portal
Pricing model Per login/member, scales with partner count Flat monthly fee
Cost as network grows Rises with every new partner Unchanged
Feature scope Broad Experience Cloud platform Built to your exact partner workflows
Data source Salesforce native Synced live to Salesforce via API

When Experience Cloud still makes sense

If partners genuinely need broad, evolving access — building their own reports, using multiple Salesforce-native features, or the network is small and stable — the native community can be the simpler path. The flat-fee case gets stronger specifically when partner count is growing, when partner needs are narrow and repetitive, or both.

To see what a flat-fee build costs against your specific partner count, use the savings calculator. The same per-login logic applies across your CRM — see the full guide to cutting CRM licensing costs, or how a custom portal moves light users off per-seat licenses.

Frequently asked questions

Does a custom partner portal replace Salesforce?

No. Salesforce stays the system of record; the portal is a purpose-built front end for your partner network that reads and writes to Salesforce through its API.

Can we migrate an existing Experience Cloud community to a flat-fee portal?

Yes — existing partner workflows and data mapping carry over; the migration replaces the licensed front end, not your underlying Salesforce data or processes.

Is this only relevant for large partner networks?

The savings scale with partner count, but the model matters most whenever partner growth is a business goal — the per-seat cost otherwise grows in lockstep with something you’re actively trying to expand.

title.rendered: Escaping Per-Member Fees in Chapter Management

excerpt.rendered: Chapter and local-affiliate management tools often bill per member, not per staff seat. Here’s why that model gets expensive as chapters grow.

content.rendered:
Multi-chapter organizations — national associations with local affiliates, franchised nonprofits, alumni networks — often use chapter management software priced per member rather than per staff seat. It’s a different billing mechanism from the per-seat CRM problem most cost-reduction advice targets, and it has a specific failure mode: the software bill grows in direct proportion to your organizational success at growing membership.

Why per-member pricing is a different problem than per-seat pricing

Per-seat software charges for the number of people using the tool. Per-member chapter software charges for the number of people the tool is about — whether or not those members ever log into anything. A national organization with 50 staff and 40,000 members isn’t paying for 50 seats; it’s paying for a rate multiplied by 40,000, regardless of headcount. Growing your membership — the actual goal of the organization — directly grows the software bill.

Where this shows up hardest

  • Rapid chapter growth. A new chapter launch or a successful membership drive can jump your per-member cost significantly in a single renewal cycle.
  • Multi-tier structures. National body, regional bodies, and local chapters each managing overlapping member data can mean paying per-member fees more than once for the same person across different system tiers.
  • Engagement-independent billing. A member who renews once a year and never logs in costs the same as one who’s highly engaged — the fee is based on membership status, not platform usage.

What to do about it

Approach What it fixes Limitation
Negotiate volume tiers at renewal Lowers the per-member rate Still scales with membership growth
Consolidate multi-tier duplicate billing Removes paying twice for the same member Requires coordination across chapter levels
Move chapter-facing functions to a flat-fee portal Decouples chapter operations from per-member billing Core national member database contract still exists

Decoupling chapter operations from the per-member meter

A lot of what chapters actually need day to day — event coordination, local officer tools, member communication for that chapter specifically — doesn’t require running through the same per-member-billed system as your national member database. A custom portal for chapter leaders and officers, synced to your national system through its API, can handle that layer on one flat monthly fee, independent of total membership count. Your national member database stays the system of record; the portal is where chapter-level work actually happens.

This is a variant of the broader problem covered in cutting association management software costs — same root issue (cost tied to something other than staff headcount), different billing mechanism. See what we build for chapter-based organizations, or run your member and chapter counts through the savings calculator.

Frequently asked questions

Can we renegotiate per-member pricing directly with our vendor?

Often, yes, particularly at volume tiers or renewal — it’s worth attempting before anything else. It typically lowers the rate rather than removing the per-member mechanism entirely, so the underlying growth curve stays.

Does a chapter portal replace our national membership database?

No. It’s built to sync with your existing national or AMS system through its API — the portal handles chapter-level operations while your core system remains the source of truth for membership records.

Does this apply to franchised or affiliate models outside traditional associations?

Yes — any structure with a national or central body plus local units billed per-member (alumni networks, franchise associations, affiliate nonprofits) runs into the same mechanism and the same options for addressing it.

Zendesk and Freshdesk both price primarily per agent seat, with cost climbing by tier for more advanced features (automation, reporting, AI tools). It gets less straightforward once the “agent” list includes people who touch tickets occasionally, seasonally, or for one narrow purpose.

Where the per-seat model strains

  • Cross-functional escalation contacts — engineering or product staff who get pulled into a handful of tickets a month, each needing a full agent seat to respond.
  • Seasonal support surges — retail, hospitality, and other seasonal businesses that need many more agents for a few weeks a year.
  • Read-only or status-check roles — managers and stakeholders who want visibility into ticket status without ever working a ticket.
  • Tier upgrades for one feature — needing a single advanced feature can push the whole team’s per-seat rate to a higher tier.

Zendesk vs. Freshdesk: the pricing shape is similar

Both platforms structure pricing the same way — per-agent, tiered by feature set — so switching between them rarely solves a per-seat cost problem; it just changes which vendor you’re paying per seat. The structural fix is the same regardless of which helpdesk you’re on.

Is switching helpdesk vendors a better fix than this?

Rarely — most mainstream helpdesk platforms price per agent seat in a similar way, so switching usually just changes the vendor, not the underlying cost structure.

title.rendered: How to Find and Remove Inactive Salesforce Users

excerpt.rendered: A step-by-step process for finding dormant Salesforce licenses, freezing them safely, and stopping them from creeping back.

content.rendered:
Every Salesforce org accumulates dormant licenses: people who changed roles, contractors whose project ended, employees who left without an offboarding ticket ever reaching IT. None of them log in anymore, and all of them are still billed at full price until someone notices. This is the cleanup process, start to finish.

Step 1: Pull last-login data

Setup → Users gives you a Last Login column, and the Login History and Identity Verification History reports go deeper if you need date ranges. Export the full user list with last-login timestamps rather than eyeballing the UI — you want a spreadsheet you can sort and filter.

Step 2: Set a dormancy threshold and flag accounts

60–90 days with zero logins is a reasonable default for most orgs — long enough to not catch someone back from parental leave, short enough to catch role changes and departures promptly. Flag anything past that threshold, and cross-reference against your HR system if you have one; a name that’s already termed in HR but still active in Salesforce is the highest-priority fix.

Step 3: Don’t just delete — freeze first

Deactivating a user in Salesforce can break record ownership, approval chains, and automation tied to that user ID. Freeze the user first (Setup → Users → Freeze), which blocks login immediately without releasing the license or disturbing ownership. Confirm nothing breaks for a business cycle, then deactivate and reassign records as needed.

Step 4: Reclaim or downgrade the license

Once a seat is confirmed dormant, either remove the license entirely (if headcount actually shrank) or hold it in a pool for the next hire rather than buying a fresh one at renewal. Either way, get the freed seat off the active bill — this is the step that’s easy to skip and expensive to forget.

Step 5: Stop it from recurring

A one-time cleanup fixes today’s bill; it doesn’t stop the same drift happening again in six months. Two things prevent recurrence: tying Salesforce deactivation to your HR/identity offboarding workflow so it’s automatic, and running a scheduled scan instead of an annual fire drill. License Guard runs this scan continuously and flags dormant and duplicate seats as they appear, so cleanup stops being a quarterly project.

Approach Frequency Effort
Manual export + review Ad hoc / annual Hours, repeated each time
Scheduled report + calendar reminder Quarterly Lower, still manual
Continuous automated scan (License Guard) Ongoing Set up once, runs itself

What this doesn’t fix

Inactive-user cleanup recovers seats you’re already paying for and shouldn’t be — it’s a maintenance task, not a structural fix. If a large share of your licensed users are active but only doing a handful of narrow tasks (checking a status, submitting a form, pulling a report), the fix is different: move them to a flat-fee custom portal synced to Salesforce instead of a per-seat license. See the full breakdown in how to reduce CRM licensing costs, and pair this cleanup with a broader look at how to identify your light CRM users.

Frequently asked questions

Will freezing a user break their existing records or workflows?

No — freezing blocks login only. Ownership, record history, and automation tied to that user ID stay intact, which is why it’s the safer first step before deactivating.

How often should we run this cleanup?

Quarterly at minimum if done manually; continuously if automated. Seat drift happens between every hiring and departure cycle, so an annual review misses months of avoidable spend.

What if a “dormant” user turns out to still need access occasionally?

That’s usually a sign they need a lighter-weight tool, not a full seat — a custom portal for occasional access costs nothing extra per person and doesn’t require reactivating a full license for infrequent use.

title.rendered: Salesforce Flow/Automation Add-On Costs vs. a Custom App

excerpt.rendered: Salesforce automation add-ons and Flow orchestration limits bill separately from seats. When a custom app costs less than staying inside the platform.

content.rendered:
Per-seat licensing is the cost most teams track, but it’s not the only meter running. Heavier automation needs — orchestration beyond standard Flow limits, external data processing, complex approval chains, integration middleware — often require add-on products or higher-tier editions, each with its own line item. At a certain point, the automation you’ve bolted onto Salesforce costs more, and does less, than a purpose-built app would.

Where automation costs hide inside Salesforce

  • Flow orchestration and API limits. High-volume automation can hit governor limits, pushing teams toward higher-tier editions or add-on API capacity.
  • Integration middleware. Connecting Salesforce to other systems often means paying for a separate integration platform (MuleSoft or similar) on top of the CRM license.
  • Add-on products. Advanced approval routing, document generation, and certain automation tools are sold as separate SKUs, each billed independently of your seat count.
  • Sandbox and environment costs. Building and testing complex automation safely often requires additional sandbox capacity, which is itself tiered and priced.

The question worth asking before adding another tool

Every add-on is a bet that the automation belongs inside Salesforce. That’s often right for logic tightly coupled to CRM records — a discount approval flow, a lead-routing rule. It’s a weaker bet when the process spans multiple systems, involves external users, or has requirements Salesforce’s automation tools weren’t built for. In those cases, the automation ends up assembled from several rented pieces instead of one tool built for the job.

Comparing the two paths

Native Flow + add-ons Custom application
Pricing Per-tier edition + per-add-on, can stack Flat monthly fee
Fit to exact process Constrained by platform automation model Built to the exact workflow
Multi-system processes Often needs separate middleware Native integration across systems

When automation needs outgrow what native Flow and its add-ons handle cleanly, a custom application replaces the stack of add-ons with one system built for the specific process — still reading and writing to Salesforce as the system of record where that’s the right call, but not paying platform-tier prices for logic that doesn’t need the platform. Does moving automation off Salesforce mean losing CRM data access?

No — a custom application built to replace add-on automation still connects to Salesforce via API when CRM data is part of the process; it replaces the licensed automation layer, not your system of record.

How do we know if our automation needs are “native” or “custom-app” shaped?

If the logic lives entirely within CRM records and standard objects, native Flow usually still fits. If the process spans multiple systems, external users, or repeatedly needs add-ons stacked together to work, that’s the signal to evaluate a custom build.

Is this a one-time migration or an ongoing relationship?

ARDN builds and runs the application on the flat monthly fee — changes to the process going forward are part of that relationship, not a new project each time.

title.rendered: Cutting HubSpot Service Hub Costs for Light Agents

excerpt.rendered: Service Hub seats price per agent. Here’s how to cut the bill for occasional and light-volume support staff without losing ticket visibility.

content.rendered:
Service Hub prices per agent seat, which is a reasonable model for a support team handling a steady ticket queue all day. It’s a worse fit for the agents who touch the queue occasionally — team leads who jump in during a spike, product staff who get looped into an escalation once a month, or seasonal support hires brought on for a launch or busy season.

Who’s paying for a full agent seat unnecessarily

  • Occasional escalation responders — engineers or product staff pulled into a handful of tickets a month.
  • Team leads and managers who review or reassign tickets but don’t own a queue themselves.
  • Seasonal or event-driven support staff whose need spikes for weeks, then drops to zero.
  • Cross-functional staff who need read access to ticket status for their own reporting, not to work tickets.

Only the first group in a support org — agents actually working the daily queue — clearly needs a full paid Service Hub seat.

Options for the rest

Use HubSpot’s lighter access where it fits

Some Service Hub tiers and permission sets allow narrower access at a lower cost than a full agent seat. Check what your tier actually offers before assuming everyone needs the same license — this alone can trim the bill for read-only or reassignment-only users.

Move narrow, recurring roles to a custom portal

For roles whose entire need is a specific slice — status visibility for a manager, a single-purpose escalation queue for occasional responders, a seasonal team working one ticket type — a custom support portal synced live to HubSpot’s ticket data gives exactly that slice, on one flat fee, whether it’s used by three people or thirty during a seasonal spike.

Role Native fit Right-sized option
Full-time queue agent Good fit Keep paid Service Hub seat
Team lead / reviewer Partial fit Lighter native tier or portal view
Occasional escalation responder Poor fit Portal, no seat
Seasonal support surge staff Poor fit — seats can’t flex down fast Portal, flat fee regardless of headcount

Why seasonal spikes are the clearest case

Seat-based pricing is built for steady headcount, not seasonal surges. Adding ten Service Hub seats for a two-month peak, then removing them, means paying full price for a temporary need — and remembering to remove them on time. A portal sidesteps that entirely: usage can spike without the bill moving, because the fee isn’t counting logins.

See the broader mechanism in cutting HubSpot seat costs, and model the numbers for your support team with the savings calculator.

Frequently asked questions

Does a support portal replace HubSpot Service Hub?

No — HubSpot stays the ticketing system of record. The portal is a synced, purpose-built front end for the roles whose need is narrower than a full agent seat.

Can this handle real-time ticket updates, or just status checks?

It depends on the scope you need — a portal can be built for live two-way ticket interaction or simple status visibility, whichever matches the role it’s built for.

Is this worth it if we only have a few occasional agents?

The savings scale with headcount and seasonality, so it matters most for teams with meaningful seasonal swings or several non-daily support touchpoints — for a very small, stable team, native tiers may already be enough.

title.rendered: HubSpot Paid vs. Free Seats: Who Needs Which

excerpt.rendered: HubSpot’s free seats aren’t as free as they sound once you factor in feature gates. Here’s how to decide who actually needs a paid seat.

content.rendered:
HubSpot markets free CRM seats prominently, and for a small team that’s genuinely useful. Past a certain size, the free-seat story gets more complicated: certain workflows, permissions, and reporting views are gated to paid seats, and teams often end up buying more paid seats than they need simply because nobody mapped who requires which features.

What a free seat actually includes

Free seats get core CRM record access — contacts, companies, basic deals — plus limited use of some tools. What they don’t get varies by hub and tier: certain custom reporting, some automation actions, and specific permission sets are paid-seat gated. The gate isn’t always obvious until someone hits it mid-task.

The three groups worth separating

  • Power users — sales reps, marketers, service agents who build sequences, run reports, and configure automation daily. They need paid seats; the features are the job.
  • Light record-viewers — managers checking pipeline, support staff looking up a contact, ops staff pulling a status. Free seats often cover this, if the permission model lines up.
  • Occasional external or narrow-task users — someone who needs one specific view or action repeatedly, but doesn’t fit either HubSpot seat type cleanly. This is the group where a seat of either kind is the wrong tool.

Where teams overpay

The common pattern: a manager or occasional user hits one paid-seat-gated feature, and rather than working around it, the team upgrades that person to a paid seat “just in case” — for a feature they’ll use once a quarter. Multiply that across a growing team and paid seats creep well past the group that actually needs them daily.

User type Right-sized option
Daily sales/marketing/service user Paid seat
Manager checking dashboards occasionally Free seat, or a lightweight portal view
One narrow recurring task (status check, form submission) Custom portal, no HubSpot seat at all
External partner/client needing a single view Custom portal

The structural option beyond seat-type audits

Auditing free vs. paid is worth doing, but it’s still working within HubSpot’s two seat types. For users whose entire need is one narrow, repeated task — checking an order status, submitting a request, viewing a single report — neither seat type is really the right shape. A custom portal synced live to HubSpot gives that exact view or action on a flat monthly fee, independent of whether HubSpot would classify them free or paid. See the full breakdown in reducing CRM licensing costs.

For the seat-cost comparison specifically, see HubSpot seat cost vs. a custom portal.

Frequently asked questions

How do we find out who’s on a paid seat but rarely uses paid features?

HubSpot’s user activity and permission reports show last-login and feature usage per seat — cross-reference against paid-seat-gated feature usage to find candidates for downgrade.

Will downgrading someone to a free seat break their workflows?

Only if they’re actively using a paid-gated feature. Confirm actual usage, not assumed usage, before downgrading — that’s the same freeze-before-deactivate caution that applies to any license change.

Does a custom portal replace HubSpot for these users?

No — HubSpot stays the system of record. The portal is a purpose-built, synced front end for users whose need is narrower than either HubSpot seat type assumes.

title.rendered: HubSpot Marketing Hub Contact-Tier Pricing Explained

excerpt.rendered: Marketing Hub bills by contacts, not just seats — a different growth curve than a per-seat CRM. Here’s how the model works.

content.rendered:
Marketing Hub’s pricing model works differently from Sales Hub or Service Hub. Instead of billing mainly by the number of people who log in, it bills largely by the number of marketing contacts in your database — a base platform fee plus additional cost as your contact count crosses tier thresholds. It’s a different growth curve, and it catches teams off guard when a successful campaign or a list import quietly pushes them into the next tier.

How the contact-tier model works

Marketing Hub plans come with a starting allotment of marketing contacts included in the base price. Once your active marketing contact count exceeds that allotment, HubSpot bills for additional contact-tier increments on top of the base tier price. Professional and Enterprise base tiers are commonly listed starting in the hundreds to low thousands of dollars per month before contact-tier add-ons — HubSpot updates these figures periodically, so confirm the current numbers on their pricing page rather than treating any figure here as current.

Why this catches teams off guard

List growth is often outside marketing’s direct control

Sales adding leads, a webinar list import, or a product signup flow can all grow the marketing contact count without marketing actively “adding” anyone — but the bill grows either way.

Non-marketing contacts can get swept in

HubSpot lets you mark contacts as non-marketing to exclude them from the billable count, but that requires someone actively managing the distinction. Left unmanaged, your marketing contact count — and the bill — includes people who were never actually part of a campaign.

Tier jumps aren’t always proportional

Crossing a contact-tier threshold can move you to a meaningfully higher monthly cost even if the number of new contacts is small relative to your total list, because tiers are priced in blocks, not per-contact increments.

Managing the cost

Lever What it does
Mark non-marketing contacts Excludes them from the billable count
Regular list hygiene (unsubscribes, bounces, duplicates) Keeps the billable count to genuinely active contacts
Route non-marketing use cases elsewhere Keeps operational/support contacts out of the marketing contact pool
Model growth against tier thresholds before campaigns Avoids surprise tier jumps mid-quarter

Where this connects to the bigger picture

Contact-tier pricing is a different mechanism from per-seat CRM pricing, but the underlying pattern is the same: cost that scales with something you don’t fully control (contact volume, headcount) rather than staying flat. The same build-vs-buy tradeoff that applies to seats applies here too — see our custom software vs. SaaS comparison for that broader framework, and how to cut CRM licensing costs for the seat-side version of this problem, including how to move light internal users off paid seats entirely — see how to cut HubSpot Sales Hub seat costs for that piece specifically.

Frequently asked questions

What counts as a “marketing contact”?

Generally, any contact you’re actively marketing to — email sends, ads audience sync, and similar. Contacts marked non-marketing are excluded from the billable count even if they still exist in your CRM.

Does deleting old contacts reduce the bill immediately?

It reduces your marketing contact count, which is what the tier is based on — but confirm how your specific plan handles mid-cycle reductions, since billing adjustments can lag the count change depending on your contract terms.

Is there a way to avoid contact-tier pricing entirely?

Not within HubSpot’s Marketing Hub — it’s a core part of how the product is priced. The lever available to you is managing which contacts count as “marketing” and keeping the list clean, not avoiding the model itself.

title.rendered: Custom Portal vs. Full CRM Migration

excerpt.rendered: Cutting CRM costs doesn’t have to mean switching platforms. Here’s how a custom portal compares to a full CRM migration.

content.rendered:
When CRM costs get painful enough, migrating to a cheaper platform entirely is one option on the table. It’s also the most disruptive one. Before committing to a full migration, it’s worth understanding what a custom portal solves without that disruption — and where migration is genuinely the right call instead.

What a full CRM migration actually involves

Moving from one CRM to another means re-mapping every custom field, workflow, integration, and report; retraining every user on a new interface; and living through a data-migration project with real risk of errors, downtime, and lost historical context. Even a well-run migration is a multi-month undertaking, and the new platform typically still bills per seat — you’re changing vendors, not changing the pricing model.

What a custom portal solves instead

A custom portal doesn’t touch your CRM at all — it syncs to it live through the API and gives specific user groups (light internal users, partners, customers) exactly the access they need, on one flat monthly fee. Your CRM stays the system of record, your power users keep working exactly as they do today, and only the light-user population moves off per-seat pricing.

Side-by-side

Full CRM migration Custom portal (keep current CRM)
Disruption High — every user, workflow, integration affected Low — power users unaffected, CRM unchanged
Timeline Months, often longer Typically weeks
Data risk Real risk of loss/errors during migration None — no data moves
Pricing model after the change Usually still per-seat, on a new vendor Flat fee for the users who move
Fixes core-team seat cost? Only if the new platform is genuinely cheaper per seat No — it targets light users, not your core team

When migration is actually the right call

If your core team’s workflow is fundamentally mismatched with your current CRM — not a cost problem but a fit problem — migration can be worth the disruption regardless of price. Similarly, if you’re locked into a platform with no reasonable path to reduce seat costs for your power users specifically, and a genuinely better-fit platform exists, that’s a real reason to migrate.

When a portal is the better move

If the actual cost driver is a large and growing population of light, external, or occasional users — not your core sales, service, or ops team — migrating the whole CRM doesn’t target the problem. It disrupts everyone to fix a cost that only a subset of users are causing. A portal fixes exactly that subset, with none of the migration risk to your core team’s workflow. See the numbers behind this in Salesforce platform license vs. custom portal, or model your own situation with the savings calculator.

Either path is a response to the same root issue covered in how to cut CRM licensing costs — the question is just which lever fits your actual cost driver.

Frequently asked questions

Can we do both — migrate the core CRM and add a portal for light users?

Yes, they’re not mutually exclusive. Some teams migrate the core platform for fit reasons and still add a portal afterward for the light-user population, since migration alone rarely fixes per-seat cost for that group.

Does a portal delay a migration decision, or replace the need for one?

It can do either. For some teams it removes enough of the cost pressure that migration stops being necessary. For others, it’s a way to control light-user cost now while a separate, unhurried migration decision plays out for the core team.

How long does standing up a portal typically take compared to a migration?

A portal build is typically measured in weeks; a full CRM migration is typically measured in months. The scope is genuinely different — a portal is a new front end synced to your existing system, not a system replacement.

title.rendered: A CFO’s Guide to Cutting Software Costs

excerpt.rendered: A framework for CFOs to cut per-seat SaaS spend without cutting the tools teams actually need — audit, right-size, then restructure.

content.rendered:
The instinct when software spend is under scrutiny is to cut seats or cancel tools — a blunt approach that risks cutting capability a team actually needs. The sturdier framework separates cost reduction into three distinct moves, each with a different risk profile, and applies them in order.

Move 1: Audit before you cut anything

You can’t right-size what you haven’t measured. Pull license counts, last-login data, and feature usage across your major SaaS contracts — CRM, helpdesk, project management, whatever else bills per seat. This step alone often surfaces dormant licenses and duplicate tools nobody flagged. See the step-by-step version in how to run a SaaS spend audit.

Move 2: Right-size within existing contracts

Before touching the tools themselves, match every user to the cheapest license tier that still covers their actual work. Most CRM and support platforms sell limited or view-only tiers below the full seat price — often unused simply because nobody mapped who needs what. This recovers real savings without changing anyone’s workflow.

Move 3: Restructure the per-seat users who don’t need a full platform

This is the move that changes the cost curve rather than just trimming it. A meaningful share of “users” on any per-seat platform — light internal staff, partners, clients — only touch it for a handful of narrow, repeated tasks. Moving them to a custom portal on a flat monthly fee turns a cost that scales with headcount into one that doesn’t, without removing their access to the underlying data.

Move Risk Typical payoff
Audit None — measurement only Surfaces dormant seats, overlap
Right-size tiers Low — no workflow change Trims existing bill
Restructure to flat-fee portal Requires a build, but keeps CRM as system of record Decouples cost from headcount growth

Why order matters

Cutting seats or canceling tools before auditing is how capability gets lost along with cost — someone loses access they actually needed because nobody checked usage first. Auditing and right-sizing first means the only people affected by the bigger structural move are the ones genuinely mismatched to a per-seat model, and they end up with a tool built for their actual job instead of a cheaper version of someone else’s.

For the specific case of CRM licensing — the largest per-seat line item for most mid-market companies — see reducing CRM licensing costs. To quantify what restructuring is worth for your team, use the savings calculator.

Frequently asked questions

How long does this whole process take?

The audit and right-sizing moves can happen in weeks with internal effort. A custom portal build for the restructuring move also runs in weeks at ARDN, not months, since the whole model is built around fast, flat-fee delivery.

Does this apply beyond CRM software?

Yes — the same three-move framework applies to any per-seat platform: helpdesk, project management, PSA tools, agency/AMS systems. CRM is usually the largest line item, which is why it’s the priority wedge.

Who should own this process internally?

Typically a joint effort between Finance (spend visibility, ROI case) and Ops/IT (usage data, workflow mapping) — neither side alone usually has the full picture needed to right-size accurately.

title.rendered: Build vs. Buy: CRM Portal for Light Users

excerpt.rendered: Weighing an off-the-shelf portal tool against a custom build for light CRM users? Here’s the honest comparison across cost, fit, and flexibility.

content.rendered:
Once you’ve decided your light CRM users (partners, clients, occasional internal staff) don’t need full seats, the next decision is how to build the alternative. Broadly there are three paths: a no-code/low-code portal builder, an off-the-shelf vertical SaaS portal product, or a custom-built portal. Each has a real, different cost and risk profile.

Option 1: No-code/low-code portal tools

Fast to stand up, and often billed per user or per active viewer — which can reintroduce the exact per-seat problem you were trying to escape, just under a different vendor. They’re also constrained to what the builder supports; workflows outside its templates get awkward fast. Good for a simple, static need; a weaker fit once the workflow gets specific.

Option 2: Off-the-shelf vertical SaaS portal products

Purpose-built for a given industry (insurance, hospitality, membership), these can fit well out of the box if your process matches the vendor’s assumptions closely. The tradeoff is the same one you’re already trying to avoid: another per-seat or per-tier subscription, plus limited ability to shape it to your exact workflow when it doesn’t quite fit.

Option 3: Custom-built portal

Built to your exact workflow, integrated directly with your CRM’s API, and — when built on a flat monthly fee model like ARDN’s — priced independently of how many users touch it. The tradeoff is upfront build time and choosing the right partner; it’s not instant like a no-code template.

No-code portal builder Off-the-shelf SaaS portal Custom build
Pricing Often per user/viewer Per-tier or per-seat Flat monthly fee
Fit to exact workflow Template-constrained Good if it matches vendor assumptions Built to spec
Time to launch Fastest Fast Weeks, not months, at ARDN
Cost as usage grows Rises with users Rises with tier/seats Unchanged

How to actually decide

The decision comes down to two questions: how standard is the workflow, and how much does usage grow over time? A simple, static need with few users can reasonably start with a no-code tool. A workflow specific to your business, or a user base (clients, partners, seasonal staff) that grows independently of your core team, is where a flat-fee custom build pays for itself — because the alternative’s cost line keeps moving with something you don’t control.

See the deeper comparison against no-code specifically in custom portal vs. no-code tool. To scope what a custom build costs for your situation, see custom portal development or run your numbers through the savings calculator.

Frequently asked questions

Is a custom build always the cheaper option?

Not always — for a very small, stable, standard use case, an off-the-shelf tool can be cheaper in the short term. The custom build wins as user count, growth, or workflow specificity increases.

How long does a custom portal actually take to build?

ARDN builds custom portals in weeks, not months — the flat-fee model is designed around fast delivery, not a multi-quarter project.

Can we start with a no-code tool and move to custom later?

Yes, and it’s a common path — validate the workflow cheaply, then move to a flat-fee custom build once the user base or workflow complexity outgrows the no-code tool’s limits.

title.rendered: Cutting Association Management Software Costs

excerpt.rendered: Association management systems bill per staff seat, per module, or per member. Here’s where the cost actually comes from — and how to control it.

content.rendered:
Association management systems (AMS platforms) run the core of most membership organizations — member records, dues, events, committees. Pricing models vary more than in most software categories: some AMS vendors bill per staff seat, some add module fees for events or committees, and some layer in per-member charges on top. Whichever combination applies to you, the bill tends to grow in ways that outpace your actual staff headcount.

Where AMS costs actually come from

Staff seats

Every staff member who touches the AMS — membership coordinators, events staff, finance — typically needs a seat, priced similarly to any per-user business software.

Module add-ons

Events management, committee management, learning management, and job boards are commonly sold as separate modules on top of the core AMS, each with its own fee.

Member-count-based fees

Some AMS platforms price partly by total member count, which means the software bill grows automatically as your association grows membership — the opposite of what you’d want a system meant to support growth to do.

Who doesn’t need a full AMS seat

Beyond the core staff running the system daily, a lot of AMS-adjacent activity comes from people who don’t need full access:

Role Typical need Right-sized option
Membership coordinator Full record management, renewals, reporting Keep full AMS seat
Committee volunteers View committee info, submit updates Portal, no AMS seat
Chapter leaders View chapter-level data, run local events Portal scoped to their chapter
Members themselves Renew dues, update profile, view benefits Portal — this is usually already how members self-serve

The structural fix

For the groups who need a narrow, specific slice of AMS data — committee volunteers, chapter leaders, sponsors — a custom portal synced live to your existing AMS through its API gives them exactly that, without adding a staff seat or triggering module fees. It’s one flat monthly fee regardless of how many volunteers or chapter leaders use it, which matters for associations where volunteer and chapter counts are large relative to paid staff headcount. Your AMS stays the system of record — this doesn’t require a platform switch.

See what we build for membership organizations at ARDN for membership organizations, or model your own numbers with the savings calculator. The underlying per-seat-vs-flat-fee math is the same one covered in cutting per-seat costs in insurance agency systems — a different vertical, same structural problem.

Frequently asked questions

Do we have to switch AMS platforms to fix this?

No. A custom portal is built to sync with your existing AMS through its API — it’s an additional front end for specific user groups, not a replacement for your core system.

Can this handle chapter-specific or committee-specific permissions?

Yes — a portal can be scoped so chapter leaders and committee volunteers only see data relevant to their chapter or committee, which is often harder to configure cleanly inside a general-purpose AMS permission model.

Does this help with member-count-based AMS fees specifically?

Not directly — those fees are typically tied to your core AMS contract terms. What a portal does address is staff-seat and module-fee growth from people who don’t need full AMS access, which is usually the larger and more controllable part of the bill.

title.rendered: How to Negotiate Your Salesforce Renewal

excerpt.rendered: A practical playbook for negotiating your Salesforce renewal — what leverage actually works, and what to bring to the table.

content.rendered:
Salesforce renewal conversations tend to go one of two ways: you accept whatever the account executive proposes, or you show up with your own numbers and a credible alternative. The second version gets meaningfully better outcomes. Here’s how to prepare for it.

Start 90 days out, not 90 minutes out

Negotiating leverage comes from having time to act on what you find — if you’re auditing seats the week before renewal, you have no room to actually deactivate or migrate anyone before the deadline. Give yourself at least a full quarter.

1. Run the audit first

You can’t negotiate from a position of strength without your own usage data. Pull last-login dates, license-type assignments, and feature usage where available. Our License Guard app automates the dormant-seat scan on Salesforce if you don’t want to build the report by hand; the full audit process is in our Salesforce license audit checklist.

2. Know your real number, not the list price

List price is a starting point for the vendor, not the number you should expect to pay. Multi-year deals, competitive pressure, and your own usage trend (flat or shrinking active-user count vs. growing) all move the number. Come in knowing exactly how many seats you actually need — not how many you’re currently paying for.

3. Bring a credible alternative, not a bluff

“Can we get a discount?” is a weak opening. “We’re moving 120 light users off per-seat licenses onto a flat-fee portal unless the per-seat price comes down” is a different conversation entirely, because it’s backed by a real plan you can execute either way. This only works if the alternative is genuine — plug your numbers into the savings calculator so the alternative has real math behind it, not just a talking point.

4. Negotiate term length deliberately

Longer terms often come with better per-seat pricing, but they lock in your current seat count and tier mix for years. If you’re mid-transition — reclaiming dormant seats, right-sizing tiers, or moving light users to a portal — a shorter term or a seat-count true-down clause protects you from paying for capacity you’re actively shedding.

5. Push for true-down rights, not just true-up

Most contracts let Salesforce add seats mid-term (true-up) but don’t let you remove them until renewal (true-down). If you’re actively reducing seat count, ask explicitly for the ability to true down at agreed checkpoints — it’s a reasonable ask, especially on multi-year terms.

6. Separate “what we use” from “what we’re locked into”

Bundles and add-ons accumulate over time. Before renewal, list every SKU on the contract and confirm someone actually uses it. Unused add-ons are pure margin for the vendor and pure waste for you — cut them before you negotiate the core seats.

Leverage point Why it works
Documented dormant/light seats Shows you know your real usage, not just your contracted count
A funded alternative (portal migration plan) Makes “we’ll walk from some seats” credible, not a bluff
Flat or declining active-user trend Undercuts the case for growth-based price increases
Unused SKUs/add-ons identified Easy cuts that don’t require any behavior change

What negotiation can’t fix

Negotiation moves the per-seat rate. It doesn’t change the fact that per-seat pricing scales with headcount forever — a great renewal this year doesn’t stop the bill from climbing again in three years as you hire. For the structural fix, see the full framework in how to cut CRM licensing costs, which covers moving light users to a flat-fee portal so the number stops growing with your team.

Frequently asked questions

How much of a discount is realistic?

It varies by org size, competitive situation, and timing in Salesforce’s fiscal quarter — there’s no universal number, and anyone quoting one specific percentage is guessing. What’s consistent is that documented usage data and a real alternative both improve your position regardless of the final figure.

Does Salesforce negotiate harder at certain times of year?

Sales teams generally have more flexibility near the end of their fiscal quarter or year, when they’re motivated to close. It’s not guaranteed, but timing your renewal conversation to align with that window doesn’t hurt.

Should we mention we’re evaluating alternatives?

Only if it’s true. A specific, funded plan — like moving a defined group of light users to a portal — is legitimate leverage. A vague threat with no follow-through plan is easy for an experienced AE to see through and can undermine your credibility in future renewals.

title.rendered: A Salesforce License Audit Checklist for RevOps

excerpt.rendered: A step-by-step checklist for auditing Salesforce license spend — find dormant seats, wrong tiers, and light users before your next renewal.

content.rendered:
Most Salesforce license audits happen once a year, right before renewal, under time pressure — which is exactly when it’s easiest to miss money. A proper audit isn’t a single question (“are we using all our seats?”); it’s a short sequence of checks that surface dormant seats, mismatched tiers, and users who never needed a full license in the first place. Here’s the checklist RevOps teams can run in an afternoon.

Before you start: pull three reports

  • User list with last-login dates — Setup → Users, or a report on the User object filtered by LastLoginDate.
  • License usage by type — Setup → Company Information shows how many of each license type you own vs. have assigned.
  • Permission set / profile assignments — so you can see who’s on a full Sales or Service Cloud profile vs. a limited one.

The audit checklist

1. Flag dormant accounts

Anyone with no login in 60–90 days is a candidate for deactivation. Cross-check against HR/offboarding records — a large share of dormant seats are simply former employees whose accounts were never removed. Tools like License Guard automate this scan continuously on Salesforce, so it doesn’t rely on someone remembering to run a report before renewal.

2. Separate dormant from light

Dormant means “not logging in.” Light means “logging in, but only touching one or two things.” Both cost you money, but they need different fixes — dormant seats get reclaimed, light users get right-sized or moved off the platform entirely.

3. Check license type against actual usage

For every active user, ask: does their day-to-day work require full Sales/Service Cloud, or would a Platform license, a login-based license, or no Salesforce seat at all cover it? It’s common to find staff on full Enterprise seats who only ever update a status field or check an order.

4. Count integration and “just in case” seats

Test accounts, integration users left over from old projects, and seats provisioned “for when they need it” all quietly bill every month. List every seat and require a name and a reason next to each one.

5. Identify external users on internal licenses

Partners, vendors, and customers sometimes end up on internal seats because it was the fastest way to get them access at the time. That’s usually the most expensive way to grant limited external access — flag every external user for a licensing review.

6. Total the reclaimable spend

Add up dormant seats × your per-seat rate for a year-one reclaim number, then separately estimate what moving light and external users off per-seat licenses would save going forward. These are two different pools of savings — one-time reclaim vs. structural reduction.

Finding Typical share of an org Fix
Dormant (90+ days, no login) ~22–34% of paid seats, per License Guard’s published benchmark Deactivate / reclaim
Wrong tier for the job Varies by org Right-size to Platform or login-based license
Light, structurally low-usage Often the majority of non-power users Move to a flat-fee custom portal
External on internal seat Common in partner/vendor programs Move to portal or external license

What the audit doesn’t fix

An audit is a snapshot — seats drift back into dormancy every quarter as people change roles or leave. Continuous monitoring (License Guard is a free app built for this) keeps the list clean between audits. And for the light-user pool the audit surfaces, right-sizing tiers only goes so far, since even the cheapest per-seat tier still bills per person. The durable fix for that group is a custom portal on a flat monthly fee, wired into Salesforce, that costs the same regardless of headcount. See the full framework in how to cut CRM licensing costs.

Once you’ve run the audit, bring the numbers to your renewal conversation — see our guide on how to negotiate your Salesforce renewal, and use the same audit method described in how to tell which CRM users you’re overpaying for to prioritize which light users to move first.

Frequently asked questions

How often should we run this audit?

At minimum, 60–90 days before every renewal, so there’s time to act on the findings. Many RevOps teams also run a lighter monthly check for new dormant accounts, especially after headcount changes.

Do we need special tooling to run this audit?

No — everything above can be pulled from standard Salesforce reports. Free tools like License Guard just automate the dormant-seat scan so it runs continuously instead of once a year.

What’s the single biggest finding audits tend to miss?

The light-user pool. Dormant seats are easy to spot and reclaim; light users who are technically active but only need a fraction of a full seat are harder to see in a login report alone, and they’re usually the largest structural cost.

title.rendered: Salesforce Experience Cloud Pricing, Explained

excerpt.rendered: How Salesforce Experience Cloud licensing actually works — login vs. member-based pricing, what it costs, and when a portal costs less.

content.rendered:
Experience Cloud (formerly Community Cloud) is Salesforce’s answer to giving partners, customers, and other external users a portal without handing them full internal seats. It’s usually cheaper than a Sales or Service Cloud license — but “cheaper per user” and “cheap at scale” aren’t the same thing, and the licensing model trips people up. Here’s how it actually works.

The two Experience Cloud licensing models

Salesforce sells Experience Cloud access two ways, and which one applies depends on the edition and use case:

Login-based licenses

You buy a pool of logins and each authenticated session draws from it. This fits low-frequency users well — someone who logs in twice a month costs a lot less than someone in the portal daily. Salesforce has publicly listed login-based Experience Cloud pricing in the roughly $2–$10 per login range depending on the license type and edition (check current Salesforce pricing for your org, since these figures move).

Member-based licenses

You pay a flat rate per named external user regardless of how often they log in — closer to a traditional per-seat model, just at a lower rate than an internal seat. This suits people who use the portal regularly, since a login-based license would rack up charges fast for a daily user.

Where the cost still adds up

Both models are cheaper per person than a full internal seat, but both still scale with the number of external users or logins you have. A partner program with a few dozen partners is inexpensive; one with a few hundred partners, plus their staff, plus your customers, starts to look like a real, growing line item — because it’s still fundamentally a per-user (or per-login) meter.

Option Typical published pricing Scales with users?
Full Sales/Service Cloud seat ~$150–$165/user/mo Yes
Experience Cloud (login-based) ~$2–$10 per login Yes — per login
Experience Cloud (member-based) Flat rate per named user, below internal-seat pricing Yes — per user
Custom portal One flat monthly fee No

Prices are publicly listed ranges as of this writing, not quotes — confirm current pricing with Salesforce.

When Experience Cloud is the right call

If your external-user population is small, relatively stable, and you want to stay entirely inside declarative Salesforce tooling, Experience Cloud is a reasonable, supported option — it’s built for this and integrates natively. The tradeoff is that you’re still on a per-user (or per-login) meter, and Experience Cloud’s page layouts and components are built for general-purpose portals, not necessarily your exact workflow.

When a custom portal wins

Once the external-user population is large, growing, or needs a workflow Experience Cloud’s component set doesn’t fit well, a custom portal — synced live to Salesforce through its API — breaks the link between cost and user count entirely. It’s one flat monthly fee whether you have 50 partners or 5,000, and it’s built around your exact process rather than a general community template. We cover the full head-to-head, including the “when each wins” cases, in our Experience Cloud vs. custom portal comparison.

For the broader picture on cutting CRM costs beyond just external users, see how to cut CRM licensing costs. And if you haven’t audited your internal seats yet, start with our Salesforce license audit checklist — internal seat waste is usually the bigger number.

Frequently asked questions

Is Experience Cloud the same as a customer portal?

It’s Salesforce’s product for building one. “Experience Cloud” is the platform; the actual site or portal you build on it (customer portal, partner portal, help center) is the “experience.”

Do login-based or member-based licenses cost less?

It depends entirely on usage frequency. Infrequent users cost less on login-based pricing; daily users usually cost less on member-based pricing. Model both against your actual usage pattern before committing to one.

Can we replace Experience Cloud with a custom portal without losing Salesforce data?

Yes. A custom portal reads and writes the same Salesforce records through the API in real time — Salesforce stays the system of record either way. The difference is the front end and the pricing model, not the data.

title.rendered: SaaS Seat Sprawl: Why Mid-Market Bills Keep Climbing

excerpt.rendered: Why mid-market software bills grow faster than headcount — and the structural fix for seat sprawl across a company’s tool stack.

content.rendered:
Ask most mid-market Ops or IT leaders why their software spend keeps climbing, and headcount growth is usually the first answer — but it’s rarely the whole story. Most companies run more tools than they think, most of those tools bill per seat, and the seat count on each one tends to only go up. That combination is what “seat sprawl” actually means, and it compounds quietly.

How seat sprawl happens

Tool sprawl across departments

Every department adopts its own tools over time — a CRM, a project management app, an HR platform, a support desk, a handful of niche point solutions. Each one is a reasonable decision in isolation. Collectively, they’re a large and growing stack of per-seat subscriptions, several of which overlap in what they actually do.

Default-to-full-access provisioning

New hires are commonly given the same access as everyone else in their department by default, rather than the specific tier or tool their actual job requires. It’s the fast way to onboard someone — and it means most orgs are provisioning more expensive access than most people use.

Offboarding lag

Seats that should be deactivated when someone leaves or changes roles often aren’t, immediately or ever. Multiply a few weeks of lag per departure across a company with regular turnover, and it adds up to real recurring waste.

External users on internal licenses

Partners, vendors, and customers frequently end up provisioned on internal, full-price seats because it was the fastest way to grant them access — not because that’s the right pricing tier for an outside user.

Why mid-market companies feel this the most

Small teams don’t have enough tools or headcount for sprawl to matter much. Large enterprises typically have dedicated SaaS management functions specifically to control it. Mid-market companies (roughly 200–2,000 employees) tend to sit in the gap: enough tools and headcount growth to make sprawl expensive, but rarely a dedicated function whose job is watching it.

Sprawl driver What it looks like Fix
Tool overlap Two+ tools doing the same job Consolidate, cancel the redundant one
Over-provisioned access Full seats for light or occasional users Right-size tiers, audit regularly
Offboarding lag Ex-employees still on active seats Tie deactivation to HR/identity system
External users on internal seats Partners/customers on full-price licenses Move to external tier or a flat-fee portal

The structural fix

Audits and consolidation trim the existing bill, but they don’t change the underlying pattern — every tool that bills per seat will keep scaling with headcount, indefinitely, no matter how clean your provisioning is. The structural fix is moving the workflows with the largest and fastest-growing user populations — usually light users touching a system for a narrow set of tasks — onto custom-built, flat-fee software instead of another per-seat subscription. We cover the underlying build-vs-buy math in custom software vs. SaaS.

Start by running your own numbers through the savings calculator, and for the general per-seat vs. flat-fee mechanics behind the fix, see per-seat vs. flat-fee software pricing, compared.

Frequently asked questions

How do we even find out how much seat sprawl we have?

Start with a simple inventory: list every SaaS tool the company pays for, who owns it, and current seat count vs. active-user count for each. Most companies are surprised by how many tools show up once someone actually compiles the list.

Isn’t this just a procurement problem?

Partly, but procurement controls new purchases — it doesn’t fix seats that are already provisioned and quietly billing. Sprawl needs both tighter intake for new tools and an ongoing audit of what’s already running.

Does consolidating tools always save money?

Usually, but not automatically — migration and change-management have real costs too. It’s worth running the math per tool rather than assuming consolidation is always the right call; sometimes right-sizing seats within a tool is the faster win.
